extracted.intended_audience: state and federal regulators, power plant owners/operators, environmental attorneys, and stakeholders responding to or implementing EPA NSPS/section 111 rules for electric generating units
extracted.subtask_short: EPA NSPS standards for power plants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rulemaking preamble explaining applicability, BSER determinations, and technical/operational criteria for new, modified, and reconstructed electric generating units (EGUs) under CAA section 111. Includes definitions, threshold calculations, subcategorization considerations, and technological/practical assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of 'standard of performance'
rubrics_metrics.description: “The term ‘standard of performance’ means a standard for emissions of air pollutants which reflects the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost of achieving such reduction and any nonair quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the Administrator determines has been adequately demonstrated.” (42 U.S.C. 7411(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying/setting standards, the EPA must consider (and balance) cost of achieving reduction, any non-air quality health and environmental impacts, and energy requirements; the Agency's BSER determination must reflect the degree/percentage reduction achievable under those constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER identified as CCS with 90 percent capture
rubrics_metrics.description: “The EPA uses the two phrases (i) BSER is CCS with 90 percent capture and (ii) CCS with 90 percent capture is achievable, or similar phrases, interchangeably.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA treats 90% CO2 capture via CCS as the best system of emission reduction for applicable sources where determined; discussions elsewhere note technical differences between coal and natural gas post-combustion capture and circumstances where CCS may be infeasible (e.g., non-base load simple cycle turbines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of operating horizon / remaining useful life for subcategorization
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may take operating horizon into account in determining whether subcategorization is appropriate; states may continue to take remaining useful life (RULOF) factors into account for particular units where the information for those units differs from EPA's bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA views operating horizon as a permissible factor when many units share similar announced shorter operating horizons; however, states retain authority to consider remaining useful life for individual units if materially different facts apply. If a court disallows subcategorization based on intended cessation dates, states could consider co-firing as an alternative through state-level factor consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base load rating criterion: capability to combust 250 MMBtu/h
rubrics_metrics.description: “The EPA refers to the capability to combust 250 MMBtu/h of fossil fuel as the ‘base load rating criterion.’ Note that 250 MMBtu/h is equivalent to 73 MW or 260 GJ/h heat input.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 250 MMBtu/h (or 73 MW) as the numeric threshold when determining whether a unit meets the base load rating criterion for applicability/subcategorization analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated equipment included in affected facility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Auxiliary equipment such as boilers or combustion turbines that provide heat or electricity to the primary EGU (including to any control equipment) would still be considered integrated equipment and included as part of the affected facility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When delineating the affected facility for NSPS purposes, include auxiliary/aux equipment that supplies heat or power to the primary EGU (and to its control equipment) as part of the regulated unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approved methods to determine design efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT currently lists “ASME PTC 22 Gas Turbines,” “ASME PTC 46 Overall Plant Performance,” and “ISO 2314 Gas turbines—acceptance tests” as approved methods to determine the design efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed ASME/ISO standards as the recognized test/measurement procedures for determining design efficiency for applicability and threshold calculations under subpart TTTT.

rubrics_metrics.name: HHV/LHV conversion and impact on efficiency thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: “The HHV of natural gas is 1.108 times the LHV of natural gas. Therefore, the HHV efficiency is equal to the LHV efficiency divided by 1.108... European plants tend to report thermal efficiency based on the LHV of the fuel rather than the HHV for both combustion turbines and steam generating EGUs. In the U.S., boiler efficiency is typically reported on a HHV basis.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether efficiencies are expressed on an HHV or LHV basis—convert using factor 1.108 for natural gas. Mixing LHV and HHV in threshold calculations changes numeric thresholds (EPA notes the mixture results in the electric sales threshold being ~11% higher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric sales threshold calculation (design efficiency + base load rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The calculation used to determine the electric sales threshold includes both the design efficiency and the base load rating. Since the base load rating stays the same when adjusting the numeric value of the design efficiency for applicability purposes, adjustments to the design efficiency has twice the impact. Specifically, using three-fourths of the design efficiency reduces the electric sales threshold by half.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When calculating the percent-electric-sales applicability threshold, account for both design efficiency and base load rating; small changes to the design-efficiency input have amplified effects on the resulting electric-sales threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of electric sales (not utilization) for applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: “While utilization and electric sales are often similar, the EPA uses electric sales because the focus of the applicability is facilities that sell electricity to the grid and not industrial facilities where the electricity is generated primarily for use onsite.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine applicability based on electric sales to the grid rather than utilization/capacity factor when distinguishing covered vs non-covered units under these NSPS provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percent electric sales, capacity factor, and annual hours categorize combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: “Percent electric sales thresholds, capacity factor thresholds, and annual hours of operation limitations all categorize combustion turbines based on utilization.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple metrics (percent electric sales, capacity factor, annual hours) are used to categorize combustion turbines into subcategories (e.g., base load, intermediate, low load) depending on utilization patterns; apply the specific threshold values in the rule text/preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: dispatchable vs. variable generating sources
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dispatchable generating sources are those that can be turned on and off and adjusted to provide power to the electric grid based on the demand for electricity. Variable (sometimes referred to as intermittent) generating sources are those that supply electricity based on external factors that are not controlled by the owner/operator of the source (e.g., wind and solar sources).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these functional definitions when considering interactions with grid operations, applicability, and potential crediting/interaction with other generation sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty cycle definition (average operating capacity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The duty cycle is the average operating capacity factor. For example, if an EGU operates at 75 percent of the fully rated capacity, the duty cycle would be 75 percent regardless of how often the EGU actually operates.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use duty cycle as the metric for average utilization when assessing categories and expected operating performance; distinguish duty cycle from the number/frequency of starts/stops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary load assumption for combined cycle turbines with 90% CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: “The 7 percent auxiliary load for combined cycle turbines with 90 percent CCS is specific to electric output. Additional auxiliary load includes thermal energy that is diverted to the CCS system instead of being used to generate additional electricity. This additional auxiliary thermal energy is accounted for when converting the phase 1 emissions standard to the phase 2 standard.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating CCS performance into an electric-output standard, include both electrical auxiliary loads (7% for the cited scenario) and diverted thermal energy impacts in phase conversions of emissions standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design efficiency cap for combined cycle turbines (50% LHV)
rubrics_metrics.description: “While the design efficiency is capped at 50 percent on a LHV basis, the base load rating (maximum heat input of the combustion turbine) is on a HHV basis. This mixture of LHV and HHV results in the electric sales threshold being 11 percent higher than the design efficiency.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 50% LHV cap where specified; be cautious mixing LHV/HHV metrics when applying the cap and when computing applicability thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-emitting fuels requirement (160 lb CO2/MMBtu)
rubrics_metrics.description: “For owners/operators of combustion turbines the lower emitting fuels requirement is defined to include fuels with an emissions rate of 160 lb CO2/MMBtu or less. For owners/operators of steam generating units or IGCC facilities the EPA is requiring the use of the maximum amount of non-coal fuels available to the affected facility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To meet the lower-emitting fuels BSER for combustion turbines, use fuels at or below 160 lb CO2/MMBtu; for steam/IGCC, maximize non-coal fuel usage subject to practical availability/limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monthly fuel-based site-specific standards for co-firing combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: “Combustion turbines co-firing natural gas with other fuels must determine fuel-based site-specific standards at the end of each operating month. The site-specific standards depend on the amount of co-fired natural gas.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners/operators who co-fire must perform monthly calculations to establish site-specific standards reflecting the actual blending proportions of fuels during that month; compliance reporting/monitoring must support this periodic determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrogen co-firing effects on subcategorization and BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: “Note that according to 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT, combustion turbines co-firing 25 percent hydrogen by volume could be subcategorized as multi-fuel-fired EGUs because the percent methane by volume could fall below 70 percent, the heating value could fall below 35 MJ/Sm3., and 10 percent of the heat input could be coming from a fuel not meeting the definition of natural gas... The EPA recognizes that standards of performance are technology neutral and that a standard based on application of CCS could be achieved by co-firing hydrogen. The EPA is not finalizing a definition of low-GHG hydrogen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hydrogen co-firing at sufficient volumetric percentages can change fuel-category status and thus applicability/subcategory assignments; EPA acknowledges hydrogen co-firing may achieve equivalent reductions to CCS in some instances but is not adopting a formal low-GHG hydrogen definition in this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly efficient generation: technology + best O&M practices
rubrics_metrics.description: “The EPA sometimes refers to highly efficient generating technology in combination with the best operating and maintenance practices as highly efficient generation. The affected sources must meet standards based on this efficient generating technology upon the effective date of the final rule.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards may be framed around the use of high-efficiency generation technologies combined with prescribed O&M practices; affected sources are expected to meet standards reflecting that combination on the effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational characteristics to minimize emissions at low load
rubrics_metrics.description: “Important characteristics for minimizing emissions from low load combustion turbines include the ability to operate efficiently while operating at part load conditions and the ability to rapidly achieve maximum efficiency to minimize periods of operation at lower efficiencies. These characteristics do not necessarily always align with higher design efficiencies that are determined under steady-state full-load conditions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating low-load performance, prioritize part-load efficiency and fast ramping capability rather than relying solely on steady-state, full-load design-efficiency metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA decision to exclude integrated renewables from BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: “The EPA did not propose to include, and is not finalizing including, integrated renewables as part of the BSER. Commenters opposed a BSER that would include integrated renewables as part of the BSER. Commenters noted that this could result in renewables being installed in suboptimal locations which could result in lower overall GHG reductions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on integrated renewables (e.g., colocated wind/solar) as part of the federal BSER determination for this source category; such measures are not part of the nationally-applicable BSER in this final action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness calculation sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The cost effectiveness calculation is highly dependent upon assumptions concerning the increase in capital costs, the decrease in heat rate, and the price of natural gas.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic evaluations of options (e.g., adding CCS or other technologies) must be accompanied by transparent assumptions about capital cost increases, expected heat-rate improvements, and natural gas price trajectories because results are highly sensitive to these inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting and construction timing assumptions for natural gas pipeline laterals
rubrics_metrics.description: “The average time for permitting for a natural gas pipeline lateral is 1.5 years, and many sources could be permitted faster (about 1 year) so that it is reasonable to assume that many sources could begin construction by June 2027. The average time for construction of an individual pipeline is about 1 year or less. Considering this, the EPA assumes construction of all of the natural gas pipeline laterals in the analysis occurs over a 2-year period (June 2027 through June 2029), and notes that in practice some of these projects could be constructed outside of this period.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cited permitting (~1–1.5 years) and construction (~1 year) timing assumptions when assessing feasibility/timelines for pipeline-dependent actions (e.g., co-firing conversions) in regulatory cost/implementation analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting electricity sold during system emergencies toward electric-sales threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: “In 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT, electricity sold by units that are not called upon to operate due to a system emergency (e.g., units already operating when the system emergency is declared) is counted toward the percentage electric sales threshold.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Units' sales during declared grid/system emergencies (variously defined by grid operators) are credited toward percent-electric-sales thresholds; applicants should account for these occurrences when calculating monthly/annual electric sales metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for combustion turbines not capable of combusting natural gas (non-contiguous areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: “40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT, also includes coverage for owners/operators of combustion turbines in non-contiguous areas. However, owners/operators of combustion turbines not capable of combusting natural gas (e.g., not connected to a natural gas pipeline) are not subject to the rule. This exemption covers many combustion turbines in non-contiguous areas.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combustion turbines physically unable to burn natural gas (often in non-contiguous areas lacking pipeline access) are exempt from the cited requirements; determine applicability based on actual fuel capability and connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: CHP net electricity sales and CHP credit for line losses
rubrics_metrics.description: “For contractual reasons, many developers of CHP units sell the majority of the generated electricity to the electricity distribution grid. Owners/operators of both the CHP unit and thermal host can subtract the site purchased power when determining net electric sales. Third-party developers that do not own the thermal host can also subtract the purchased power of the thermal host when determining net electric sales for applicability purposes... 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT, provides a way to account for the environmental benefit of reduced line losses by crediting CHP EGUs, which are typically located close to large electric load centers. See 40 CFR 60.5540(a)(5)(i) and the definitions of gross energy output and net energy output in 40 CFR 60.5580.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When calculating net electric sales for CHP units, subtract site-purchased power consistent with contractual/ownership arrangements; apply subpart TTTT provisions to account for reduced line losses (CHP credit) per the cited regulatory provisions.
